subsubtopic: KINGSTON PENITENTIARY-REPORTED REJECTION OF BOOK DONATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to bring to the attention of the House the recent ridiculous situation at the Kingston Penitentiary. Chuck Armstrong, Secretary of the Inmate Committee, dared to write a letter to The Toronto Star asking for donations of used books for the prison library. Not only did the prison warden refuse to accept the books, the inmate was thrown off the prisoners' committee for writing a letter to The Toronto Star, as the secretary of the committee, without having the expressed approval of the prison.
Illiteracy is a widespread problem, particularly among our prisoners. Where is there justification at Kingston Penitentiary in refusing books that libraries and citizens are more than willing to donate when there exists an amazingly high percentage of illiterates among the prison population, and when this is the Year of Literacy in Canada?
I call upon the Solicitor General of Canada (Mr. Kelleher) to have Mr. Armstrong reinstated and begin accepting books at the Kingston Penitentiary. What with the Prime Minister's (Mr. Mulroney) decision to build a prison in Port-Cartier at such expense, any donation to prisons should bring a sigh of relief to the Government.

subsubtopic: NEED TO IMPROVE SURVEILLANCE OF EMPLOYEES' PENSION FUNDS BY DEPARTMENT OF INSURANCE
speechtext:
In his latest report, Mr. Speaker, the Auditor General mentions that the Department of Insurance regulates about 560 insurance, trust and loan companies with over-all assets of over $200 billion, and 750 employer-sponsored pension plans valued at $28 billion.
His audit has revealed that the Department of Insurance surveillance of pension plans is a lot less strict than it is with respect to financial institutions. He points out that current surveillance methods do not allow him to have enough control over the solvency of pension plans, so much so that department officials could indeed improve considerably their monitoring of financial institutions.
They should also devote more time to forecasting future trends in this sector and singling out new sectors which may present some risks.
Therefore it is imperative to exercise stricter control over these institutions to prevent surpluses from being used for private investments and avoid speculation with the pension funds of employees, as was the case with respect to Argus Corporation President, who used those funds to buy a daily newspaper in England.

subsubtopic: NON-PAYMENT OF INCOME TAX BY COSEKA RESOURCES LIMITED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the recipient of our tenth great untaxed corporation award is Coseka Resources Limited. This company's ability to use generous Liberal and Conservative tax concessions has resulted in current tax credits in every year from 1978 to 1981 on millions of dollars of profits. From 1982 to 1985 the company was granted the right to pay no income taxes at all on $33 million in profits. Had the tax system been fair and equitable, and had this company been required to pay a tax rate of 25 per cent on its profits, Canadian taxpayers would have had their tax bill reduced by $8.2 million.
Canadians are looking for real action in the area of tax reform, not simply more consultation and vague promises about reform for another two years, as was indicated by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) yesterday.

subsubtopic: ANNIVERSARY OF ORGANIZATION'S FOUNDATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today is United Nations day. We would do well to remember the purpose for which the United Nations was founded. Forty-one years ago, as the world was emerging from six years of war, it was set up to create a system for the maintenance of international peace and security. In meeting that basic objective, the international community has, on balance, succeeded, but much still remains to be done. So long as people go unfed, so long as men and women are imprisoned for their beliefs, and so long as the world is threatened by violence and war, no nation or individual can afford to cease working for a better society.
There could be no better way for Canadians to mark this anniversary than by recommitting ourselves to the principles of the United Nations Charter and to the strengthening and revitalization of the organization. Let our renewed commitment be an example to all member states.

subsubtopic: SITUATION OF SINGLE, ELDERLY AND HEADS OF FAMILIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in their report entitled Progress Against Poverty the National Council of Welfare point to a significant decline in Canada's poverty rate among men and the elderly. While the over-all situation is improving, however, single and elderly women and others who are heads of families are getting ever poorer. Indeed six out of 10 single-parent families headed by women live under the threshold of poverty. The poverty rate among single mothers did not decrease in 1985. In this category poverty has been gradually worsening over the past five years. A single mother is five times more likely than a married woman to end up swelling the ranks of the poor. Inequality among single-parent families is glaring. A single-parent family headed by a woman stands four times as many chances of being poor as a family headed by a man.
In the light of this depressing situation, Mr. Speaker, allow me to say that the comments made last October 21 by the Minister responsible for the Status of Women were particularly ill-chosen; she stated that surely the Conservative Government has done something to improve the status of women in Canada, considering that a few women have been able to sit on Government benches-

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT MEASURES TO SUPPORT AND ENCOURAGE THE DISABLED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, some 3.5 million Canadians are disabled. This represents some 14 per cent of our population, virtually one person in seven. In spite of inherited financial difficulties, this Government has taken a number of positive steps to support further and encourage the handicapped.
The funding for the disabled persons' program will increase fivefold. A new housing renovation program will raise the maximum subsidy from $1,500 to $5,000. The flat rate disability payment will rise from $87 per month to $224 per month effective January 1, 1987. A broader definition of "disability" will enable an additional 120,000 Canadians to secure an income tax deduction, a deduction which has been increased by $250 this year.
These initiatives, which improve the living conditions of the disabled, are an integral part of the ongoing thrust of the Government toward greater social justice for all Canadians.

subsubtopic: ARRIVAL OF RICK HANSEN IN OTTAWA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I know all Members of Parliament would want to join me in welcoming Rick Hansen to the National Capital today. He is an exceptional Canadian who has now travelled through 34 countries, including the Soviet Union, China, and Australia, a distance of 40,000 kilometres, on his Man in Motion Tour.
Rick Hansen has simply set out to prove that people who are disabled can realize their dreams, that life does not stop because of disability. He has been seeking to change the perception of Canadians and people around the world about those who are disabled. The disabled are our peers. They are our equals.
I, personally, as the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre, want to pay tribute to Rick Hansen for the courage and the perseverance he has shown following in the footsteps, if I may say, of his friend, Terry Fox. I wish him well on his very difficult journey for the rest of the Man in Motion Tour until he reaches Vancouver.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is addressed to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: OBSERVANCE OF SANCTIONS AGAINST SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me thank the Hon. Member for his question, both today and two day's ago. After his original question I spoke to Mr. Pierre Jeanniot, President of Air Canada. Air Canada, in fact, did not act in any way that undermines the sanctions policy of the Government of Canada. Accordingly, Air Canada will no longer be involved in facilitating travel to and from South Africa.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today I would like to address the issues of social justice and issues related to women. In the context of the Speech from the Throne I would like to read into the record the remarks of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) who, with compassion and understanding, described the goals of the Government on matters of social justice. He said:
My government will continue to enlist the support of all in pursuit of the common goal: a modern, tolerant, and caring nation in which its citizens are secure and prosperous. Canadians would want their governments to give the highest priority in social policy to those who are in greatest need. As well, Canadians expect to enjoy the highest quality in health care and other social benefits that have become fundamental to our national quality of life.
When I reflect on those remarks I must say that we have come a long way since the Parliament of 1974 to 1979 when my colleagues and I, and in particular the distinguished Hon. Stanley Knowles, repeatedly espoused the cause of widows, spinsters and other women in like condition, that major element of society which lives below the poverty line. Their condition has been improved, but not by the Government of that time which remained entirely insensitive to the pleas, urgings and requests of Members of Parliament from our Party and from the NDP.
We can see them today still, those who are in this unfortunate condition. We see them in supermarkets-quiet, proud, dignified, and poor. We see them as they examine the contents of their change purses before they take their purchases to the check-out counter. They look at the figures on the till adding up and they look at the nature of the food that they can afford. We all know that while we are clearly better off than many nations there are still those in that an element of society who continue to have to ration themselves both in terms of quantity and quality of food.
When I think back to the proceedings of the Standing Committee on National Health and Welfare in the period 1974-79, I can only say that it was a dusty demonstration of concern ignored by an insensitive Government. Speaking of insensitivity, it should be noted for the record that at that time it was the Hon. Marc Lalonde, the former Minister of National Health and Welfare, who represented a profligate Government which was insensitive to this type of need.
Anomalies still exist within this group. Our Government has passed legislation that extends eligibility for the spouses' allowance to an additional 50,000 low-income widows. This has been most helpful in capturing a major portion of society that has been in difficulty. The question has been addressed on many occasions, how we will manage the balance. I think that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) has addressed that issue, both in the sense of his appreciation and understanding of the problem and in describing how he would seek to resolve it. On February 4, 1985, the Minister of Health said, as reported in Hansard, the following:
This Government is the first to acknowledge that there are other near-elderly persons in need who remain excluded from the important financial protection provided by the spouse's allowance program. However, as was recognized by the
The Address-Mr. Brisco
all party Task Force, the Government of Canada, in other words the Canadian people, cannot at this time go much beyond the proposals we have made.
What we can do and must do, given current economic circumstances, is to take this next logical step in extending the spouse's allowance program. The other most logical step after this legislation is seriously to take the pension reform proposals that have been made by both the task force and by other groups and give them life over the course of the mandate of this Government.
Nothing could be more heartening than to understand that there is a Minister of Health with an understanding of these conditions who indicates his intention, given the first opportunity, to address that particular circumstance. There are many benefits, the system of benefits of spouses' allowance, widows' pensions and CPP that escape this element of society. I say it is important that we address them, that they be included in the social safety net at the earliest possible opportunity.
There are other groups in society who need help. I would like to quote again the words of the Prime Minister as set out in the Speech from the Throne. He said, again in the area of social justice, the following:
Canadians are becoming increasingly aware of the suffering of battered women. This intolerable affront to human dignity and personal security compels my government's commitment to work with the provinces to implement on an urgent basis the most effective means and methods of action.
Clearly, the most effective means and method of action is to encourage the provinces to increase significantly their funding to transition homes for battered women. This increase, to be matched by the Government of Canada under the Canada Assistance Plan, is a part of the federal-provincial cost-sharing plan.
Further, the provision of a means test in this circumstance should be removed. Battered women come from all walks of life, from positions of poverty to positions of wealth, from women who are childless to women with children, either one or several. In many cases when a battered woman flees the threatening home environment she flees with no possessions, no suitcase filled with clothes, no purse with money. She leaves with only the clothes on her back and her children clutched in her arms. There is nothing there, nothing else for her. I could never be convinced that, given this type of circumstance those women who may come from a home that is comfortably well-off, or wealthy, should be subjected to a means test. Are we to say, "Yes, you can stay here, but after three or four days we expect you to start carrying your weight"? Let us hope that in a circumstance of that nature the family problems will be sorted out and resolved, and that those women who are in a position to afford the type of care that a transition home can provide will ultimately make a contribution.
The record shows that this problem crosses all elements of society, rich and poor alike. The Women In Need Society of Trail, British Columbia, makes an amazingly excellent contribution to the emotional and physical hurts of women in need in Trail and district. I say an amazing contribution because excellent care is provided with such limited resources. I have had the opportunity to visit that home on a couple of

October 24, 1986
The Address

Mr. Brisco
occasions and I have been very impressed, not only with the facility itself but with what has been done with the limited resources available. Therefore, I would be the very first to endorse a program which provides in a meaningful way for federal and provincial assistance for these people.
I have spoken of women who are in need and who need care when they are being threatened or battered. I have spoken of that element of society composed of people who are 50 to 65 years of age and who do not have a social safety net. There is a third element of society of which I would like to speak. One might say that I am changing gears regarding the groups of which I am speaking.
I would like to speak now of the deaf, the profoundly deaf and the inadequacies of the appeal system as well as the failure to understand the true nature of the disorder of the deaf. I speak of the deaf in the context of applications or appearances before appeal boards when a decision has been rendered that an individual does not qualify for a Canada Pension Plan disability benefit.
Let me tell the Elouse of but one example. About two or three years ago now, one of my constituents was discharged from his employment with the Canadian Pacific Railway because a foreman had spotted him wearing a hearing aid. When one works in the railway business and is around railway cars, hearing aids are not permitted. I can understand at least in part the need for such a regulation, and more particularly when a test will ultimately determine that the hearing aid itself is of little benefit to the victim.
After 17 years of service, my constituent was discharged. Efe had no other means of support. He was not skilled in other fields. When he made his first appeal, it was determined that because he hunted and used a rifle, like I do and like many other Members of the House and our constituents do, his habit of sighting his gun and doing occasional target practice was what had most materially contributed to his deafness. The fact that in his early life he worked on farms and with farm equipment that can clearly be demonstrated as affecting hearing was also raised. What was carefully ignored, in my view, was the level of decibels to which this man was subjected both in engines and cabooses of trains. That was not a consideration, yet clearly that was the source of the greatest volume of noise.
Regardless of those circumstances, I would like to tell the House what happened when this man appealed before an appeal board. An expert witness whom I had been able to retain described to the appeal board the nature of this man's disability and how he was affected by it. There was also a Crown witness who testified, a physician who had never examined this man but who had examined his records. When the Crown witness was asked as a physician what this man
could do for a useful occupation, she said that he could be a commercial painter and could do sand blasting. She also pointed out that the man would have to wear ear-muffs while he was doing this to protect his hearing. The fact is that the minute he put on ear-muffs, he would have no hearing at all. He would be totally deaf. If he were to have some hearing so that he could hear the cry of someone else or a word of caution, he would have to remove the protective ear-muffs. The noise of spray painting and the machinery that operates it as well as the sand blasting would increase and aggravate the deafness.
Given the fact that he could not very well do painting and sand blasting, the physician suggested that he would make a good gunsmith. She suggested that because he hunted. I wonder how many hunters are familiar enough with their guns to properly disassemble them. Certainly this man had an awareness of his rifle but that clearly does not make him a gunsmith or an apprentice-gunsmith.
When my expert witness was asked what gainful employment this man could have, his response was, and I suppose it was ironic and perhaps a touch sarcastic given the previous testimony, "Well, Your Honour, he could probably address envelopes and seal them". That statement spoke volumes about the condition of this element of society. The deaf and the profoundly deaf are ignored by those of us who have that treasured gift of hearing.
The doctor who served as a witness on behalf of this individual said something to me which I found very profound and shocking. He said: "If I had a choice to make, and thank God I have never had to make it, between having a child who is deaf or a child who is blind, I would choose blindness over deafness because having the ability to hear provides the ability to communicate and opens the world whereas deafness is a lifetime of loneliness".
What is not understood in so many of these cases is that simply turning up the volume on a hearing aid does not solve the problem. Turning up the volume, although it increases the volume, also increases the distortion heard by a deaf person. A deaf person does not hear noise the way you and I would hear it, Mr. Speaker. It is totally distorted and is like moving the radio off the station.
What I seek to put to the Government, the House and my colleagues is that this is one area for which we need more advocacy to Parliament. I urge Hon. Members to consider that. I urge Hon. Members to talk to the organizations in their constituencies which deal with the deaf and profoundly deaf. I submit that under the disability provisions of the Canada Pension Plan, the deaf and profoundly deaf are dealt with unfairly, and I think we should resolve that problem.

Mr. Speaker, 1 want to compliment my colleague on his presentation to the Chamber this morning. I was particularly impressed by the fact that he chose social justice, particularly because of the importance of that role as it relates to battered women. It was a very reflective presentation that he made to the House.
I noted in passing that in his presentation he touched upon the role of volunteers in the community. We all should note that this was a highlight in the Speech from the Throne. In my own community volunteers are very important and vital persons. They operate our local libraries, and our local fire departments. They run most of our recreation programs in minor sports. They are deeply involved with local historical societies and local museums which are dramatically important in reminding us of our culture and our heritage. Volunteers are very important persons in my community.
I was delighted that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and his Ministers saw fit in the Speech from the Throne to find ways of highlighting the role of volunteers. Will the Hon. Member comment further on the significance in his eyes of volunteerism in Canada, particularly in his constituency?

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to reply. Last weekend in my constituency, in Castlegar, I listened to an address by a woman who was very well informed
The Address-Mr. Brisco
on the subject of volunteerism. She was speaking to a large group of people principally interested in recreation, but who were involved in volunteerism in the community. Her speech was to provide the volunteers with an opportunity to attract others, and sell volunteerism. One of her remarks that I thought was both thoughtful and profound was that many years ago civilization started with the agricultural revolution. After the agricultural revolution we moved into an industrial revolution. From the industrial revolution we moved today into what is known as a period of energy revolution. She then went on to say something that really struck home: "By the year 2000, I submit to you that we will move into a new revolution, a revolution of humanitarianism." The volunteers in our communities must and will be a vital part of that. We have all heard the trite phrase that you only get out of something what you put into it. That may be trite, but it is certainly very appropriate in terms of volunteerism. I am delighted that our Government is taking every initiative open to it to encourage that particular philosophy, the philosophy and the principle of volunteerism.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I would like to congratulate my good friend and colleague, the Hon. Member for Kootenay West (Mr. Brisco), on the excellent points he made on the improved social programs that have been introduced since 1984. I would like to take this opportunity to put on the record the excellent work that this Government has done on behalf of Canada's veterans.
One of the most beneficial programs to veterans is the Aging Veterans Program which was introduced a number of years ago. We have improved on that. The name of this program is now called the VIP program, or the Veterans Independence Program. This program helps veterans stay in their own homes, therefore, they do not have to be placed in institutions. Since we took office, another 18,000 veterans over the age of 65 and in receipt of War Veterans Allowance became eligible for the program as of January 1, 1986. We will be expanding on that particular program.
There has been other legislation passed since we formed the Government. We have the improvements for compensation for former prisoners of war. We have improved the Children of War Dead (Education Assistance) Act. We have also improved the Canadian Pension Commission and the Pension Act. The Veterans' Land Act has also been improved. Veterans' widows are now eligible for VLA assistance. We have improved the War Veterans Allowance Act. This program provides financial assistance on an income-tested basis for veterans and their survivors. This is certainly a great improvement to the problems we had with the previous administration, where we had great difficulty getting pension applications processed. It was taking up to seven years to process pension applications. We have streamlined that dramatically and we are now processing veterans pension programs within months, not years. This has been well received. We also passed Bill C-28, an Act to amend the Pension Act, containing long overdue amendments. This will benefit veterans and their families.

October 24, 1986
The Address-Mr. McCurdy
These important changes came about within six months of our taking office.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) spoke to me personally when he formed the Government and became Prime Minister. He told me one of his first acts would be to allot an additional $22 million toward veterans' pensions. He fulfilled that promise and that was the start. A great deal of additional money has been provided for veterans through improvements to their pensions. I have been involved in veterans' problems for the last 14 years, and I have received a lot of mail during that time. Very rarely today do I receive a letter from a veteran about a pension, because we have improved the conditions within the Department of Veterans Affairs. This should be on the record to show the excellent performance of the Government in helping out war veterans across Canada.

speechtext: The Hon. Member for Windsor- Walkerville (Mr. McCurdy).

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
It is a
pleasure to participate in the Throne Speech debate for the second time. I would like to talk from the perspective of the City of Windsor in that the southernmost part of our country. It is a city that is almost embedded within the territory of our neighbours to the south. The implications of this location are not often appreciated by the rest of Canada. Sometimes Windsor feels as isolated from central Canada, Toronto, Montreal, and Ottawa, as from parts of the west and parts of the east.
When Governments send out tour groups to significant Canadian industrial cities and forget Windsor, again our isolation, the apparent unconsciousness about our existence, and our peculiarities are emphasized. We can reflect upon the fact that Air Canada and VIA Rail often seem to regard us as easily dismissible. This often leads to significant errors. For example, the rather cavalier nature of the treatment of Windsor by Air Canada. Its treatment should have been based upon the abundant market in that area as represented by Windsor combined with Detroit. However, Air Canada flights were cut, leading to the development of a market in Detroit for Republic Airlines. Now the situation is that Air Canada lacks what could have been a very lucrative market, while Republic Airlines flies eight hours per day between Detroit and Toronto and often offers the public a much more convenient route
between Ottawa and Windsor than the ones offered by Canadian carriers.
We sometimes feel isolated. We are sometimes puzzled by the reaction of others in Canada to our situation. We are often accused of having an American accent, as if being where we are and talking as we do somehow makes us less Canadian than other Canadians. If we compare, as we did yesterday within the context of our knowledge of the United States which is much more intimate than that of most Canadians, some of the things occurring in the United States with our own situation, we are accused of being too pro-American. On the other hand, if because of our familiarity with the United States we criticize it or. express reservations about bilateral trade negotiations, we are accused of being anti-American. Of course it is an absurdity. Windsor, with all its isolation and with all the ignorance in the rest of Canada it must face about what we are like, what we do, and what goes on there, really has the same concerns as the rest of the country. Some of the decisions and some of the policies of the Government of Canada are brought to crystal clear focus there.
The Government has chosen as its mechanism for economic development to place a huge focus-indeed, we would suggest that it is an imbalanced focus-upon opening our borders with the United States to free trade. Often we hear, this town which has benefited so much by the Auto Pact, how the Auto Pact represents the model of what we are trying to achieve across the broad spectrum of trade. We are puzzled by this. On the one hand we are puzzled because the Auto Pact represents a trade arrangement with certain rules in respect of Canadian content and employment. On the other hand, we do not see this sort of thing being aimed for in the bilateral trade negotiations. We think that they are a mistake because we should be facilitating international trade, multilateral trade.
If we look around us we see that the Government is undermining the very model it would present to the world as the model of what can be achieved in the negotiations with the United States. We see offshore producers from Japan and Korea coming into the country, often with the financial inducement of Governments, to assemble automobiles under circumstances where parts are not being manufactured or acquired in Canada. This is in contrast to what happens in respect of domestic manufacturers regulated by the Auto Pact.
Although we in Windsor feel particularly concerned about the issue, we are not the only ones who are concerned. We see the unions involved. We see the chief domestic manufacturers, such as Ford, Chrysler, and GM, asserting that this represents a danger to the domestic automobile industry and to employment in an industry which provides jobs, not only by automobile assembly, but by parts and machine tool manufacturing. The same fact has been reiterated by those who represent parts manufacturers and machine tool manufacturers.
It is not as if we were crying foul only from Windsor and only among a minor sector of the community. It has been repeatedly called to the attention of the Government that in the economic context the present demand for automobiles will
October 24, 1986

not go on forever. There will certainly be over-production in the future, creating a situation in which we will be trading one job for possibly three jobs produced by domestic manufacturers.
We are concerned about this rather conflicting message which is communicated to us about the Auto Pact. On the one hand it is used as a model, and on the other hand actions are taken which would undermine it. We understand that in a completely free bilateral trade environment between Canada and the United States there is little likelihood, under the rationalization processes in which major American companies are engaged, they would allow for very long the continuation of manufacturing by their subsidiaries in Canada. When we think about that, we think about the hundreds, nay the thousands of jobs over the years which have been lost in Windsor by virtue of decisions made in the interest of rationalization by American management. These decisions will be repeated many times over in a future free trade environment with the United States.
The Government introduced and passed the Investment Canada legislation which increased the measure of American ownership of our plants and increased the power they had in respect of the jobs of our citizens. When we note that so far this year there has been a 50 per cent increase in the rate of acquisition of Canadian companies by American owners, we wonder if the Government has a notion of where the real potential for economic development resides.
The day before yesterday during the opposition day debate on science and technology policy, I said that, viewed from the perspective of the need for Canada to develop a science and technology based industrial future, free trade is perhaps the last thing we should be seeking. We should not be looking at Washington and New York for answers to our economic development problems. We should be looking at home, at the creativity of our own people, at what can be done with our own resources, at the enhancement of our creative ability, and at what knowledge can do as a tool within the confines of our own country, before looking elsewhere to create future employment and future economic growth.
Surely the argument can be made, Mr. Speaker, and it is an argument that I would advocate, that we should not even contemplate entering into a free trade arrangement with the United States until we are in a position to compete with the Americans scientifically and technologically, and until we are able to make our resources work for us by virtue of knowledge. We should not open ourselves up to what could be an abortion of our science and technological growth by the massive quantities of moneys available to the Americans through investment and defence research, constituting 77 per cent of American government investment in research. We cannot now compete against that and ensure the survival of those who are necessary for our future.
The Address-Mr. McCurdy
Although we have a number of concerns as well, we are representative of the rest of the country, though we are far from the consciousness of so many in government and elsewhere. We have, for example, serious concerns about the environment. We are conscious of the agreement between the President of the United States and our Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) on the issue of acid rain. This is an agreement that demonstrated, not so much how much progress we have made on trans-boundary pollution but how little we have in controls to ensure that what goes into the air from United States factories will not hurt citizens here.
We have been frustrated for weeks because the City of Detroit is about to construct a huge incinerator, an incinerator that lacks the essential controls to ensure that the citizens of Windsor will not be subject to poisoning from the atmosphere from the burning of garbage in Detroit. Yet we find that not only has the Environment Protection Agency in United States been ineffectual, there is little on the basis of which one can mount an effective fight. At least so far there have been no solutions forthcoming.
We need to have sound agreements on trans-boundary pollution that will protect not just those of us in Windsor but citizens of Canada generally. Quite fairly it has to be said that there is an interest on the part of the citizens in the United States that our air pollution will not descend upon them. One should look at already existing agreements with respect to the Great Lakes water quality. We should consider the scandal of pollution in the St. Clair River. Then we should look at the failure of the international water quality agreement to do its job effectively. In order to bring about an effective solution to the problems already identified, it will cost us about $8 billion by the mid-1990s. We should consider the basic ineffectiveness of our agreement so far to deal with the problems we have in the Niagara area, in the St. Clair basin area. This situation gives us pause with respect to what will be necessary to ensure that the battle of air pollution will be fought to a successful end.
It should be said about the area represented by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor (Mr. Langdon) and myself that the area is extremely flat. You would not want to go there for downhill skiing, Mr. Speaker. You could only contemplate cross-country skiing. I should say this too, that the land is not only flat but it is low, and it could fall victim to serious flooding. Lake levels have risen to unprecedented levels. We have repeatedly in this House, as have others in our community, called attention to the need to take effective action in the face of, if not present danger, certain future danger, from serious Great Lake flooding. We have asked that the broad question of how to control the levels of the lakes be looked at to determine the degree to which they can be controlled. We have also asked that the federal Government engage with the provincial Government and the municipalities to ensure that not just those who live on the shores of the lakes but those who live in Essex county and nearby counties living considerable distances from the lake will not have their lands

October 24, 1986
The Address-Mr. McCurdy
flooded or towns destroyed because of a failure to deal adequately with this very serious problem which affects both sides of the border.
This is an international issue, a municipal issue and a provincial issue. Related to environmental questions in one part of our city, in the Turkey Creek watershed area, we have a serious problem of biological pollution derived from the fact that most homes in that area are using septic tanks. The only way this situation can be corrected is by considerable investment. Something in the order of $35 million will be needed to correct it. This is an environmental problem of serious concern to our particular municipality; but it signifies the kinds of problems that so many municipalities in this country have, of serious infrastructure deficiencies for which they have no funds to correct. They have looked to the federal Government as you know, Mr. Speaker, and have asked for the expenditure of some $10 to $12 billion dollars over the next five or ten years to address some of the infrastructure deficiencies that our cities have. I think this is a matter that the Government should look at seriously, not only on its own merits but from the point of view that there are serious unemployment problems, and a need for economic development, and an important contribution the Government could make would be to ensure that those needs are met. This should not be done simply by the unilateral provision of funds, but in co-operation with the municipalities that are willing to pay their share and the provinces that ought to pay their share.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Member for Windsor- Walkerville (Mr. McCurdy) and I both have very large ports in our ridings. A lot of people residing in both of our communities work in the United States. In view of his attack on free trade, would he advocate that the border be closed and that people living in Canada not be allowed to work in the United States?

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have had occasion previously to comment on the necessity for reasonableness in debate. The Member knows, of course, that the issue to which he refers is one of immigration. It should, however, be recognized that there are problems appearing at a number of border areas because both Canada and United States have imposed limits on the extent to which we will receive immigrants or temporary workers in our jurisdictions.
I would call to the attention of the Speaker the fact that workers are being imported from the United States to Windsor, through the misapplication of immigrant rules, to carry out skilled trade work which Canadians could well do. From time to time we have had occasion to call attention to that circumstance which we consider to be a serious problem in the construction field in particular. Time after time the construction trade unions have called attention to the far too facile provision of licences for such workers to work in Canada.
My constituency shares problems similar to those which the Hon. Member has cited, but I repeat that the issue of working in Detroit when one lives in Windsor and vice versa is quite distinct from the issue of free trade. We look forward to a serious debate on free trade rather than the irrelevant issues which might be raised with respect to that topic when it comes into question.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a couple of comments on some of the points raised by the Hon. Member for Windsor-Walkerville (Mr. McCurdy). During his debate he said several things about the Windsor-Essex County area. I am very proud to represent the area of Essex County along with Kent County. I would not like the House to be left with
October 24, 1986

the impression that the Windsor area is up to its neck in water, although that is partially true, that there is an incinerator in Detroit spewing pollution into the Windsor area and that we have a very bad air transportation system making it very difficult to get down to that forgotten land. The Hon. Member seems to want to portray Windsor as an area which has been forgotten by the Government.
I am sure it was an omission by the Hon. Member that he did not point out that in the past two years the Windsor area has been one of the greatest recipients of the prosperity brought forward by the Government. Unemployment in that area is down to approximately 5 per cent. When this Government came into office the unemployment rate was approximately 13 per cent. I am sure the Hon. Member knows that. That area has also been the recipient of several IRDP grants with the automotive industry expanding and new companies being brought in. 1 would not like the Hon. Member to speak lowly of the Windsor-Essex County area. We want to encourage people to go there and see the prosperity which the Government has brought to it.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as is so often the case, my hon. colleague from Essex-Kent has missed the point. The intent of my speech was to demonstrate that Windsor does experience a certain isolation from the rest of Canada, largely in terms of the knowledge which this and previous Governments have about our neck of the woods. However, I would like to make it clear that not only is Windsor much warmer than most parts of Canada, the hearts as well of the people there are much warmer than in other parts of the country.
I believe my hon. colleague attempts to exaggerate the role of Government in that area. He indicated that Windsor, along with other communities of the country, has been the beneficiary of certain programs. It is true that Windsor has a relatively low rate of unemployment. However, the suggestion that Windsor is experiencing its present prosperity as a result of federal government initiative could only come from someone who fails to read the newspapers or fails utterly to understand the economic situation in which the country finds itself and, most importantly, fails to understand some of the initiatives which the Government has failed to take with respect to the Auto Pact, which failures could seriously affect our city in the future. Surely the most valid test of the validity of this interjection will come at the next election when we revert to our usual pattern in Essex County of not having one single Conservative Member.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member does not seem to believe that unemployment has come down since the Government came to power, but I think he will have to admit that. Prior to the last election Windsor had the distinction of having three Liberal Cabinet Ministers located in that area. Were things better under those three Ministers than they are now?
The Address-Mr. Valcourt

Mr. Speaker, I am often astounded by the claims made by the Government about events that have occurred since its entry into power. I suppose the next thing for which the Government will claim credit is the fact that we have had more rain this year than last year.
I am certainly not standing here before you, Mr. Speaker, to defend the record of three Liberal Cabinet Ministers who we had in Windsor. I would ask the Government to undertake a serious policy study so it may come to the conclusion, as so many have, about what is appropriate for Windsor's future. I have said it is true that the unemployment rate of Windsor is presently at a relatively low level. However, it is not inevitable that the low unemployment rate will remain unchanged. It is clear that there will be changes with respect to the automotive industry. The generation of over-capacity in particular will severely change the automobile industry in Windsor and other parts of this country. Therefore we must have an industrial strategy that is not based on central decision-making in Ottawa, or free trade, or any of the other simple answers of the past. There must be more emphasis on providing local communities the wherewithal to engage in future economic planning so they may use their resources to develop a new economic future that will enable them to replace the jobs that will inevitably disappear in the automobile industry, particularly if the Government continues its present policies.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am pleased with this opportunity today to take part in the debate on the Speech from the Throne, in my capacity as Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism.
I may point out that this Speech from the Throne reiterates our Government's strong and continuing commitment to two important sectors of our economy: small business and tourism.
Mr. Speaker, the Speech from the Throne revolves in part around the theme of entrepreneurship and the entrepreneurial spirit which this Government sees as the principal tool for the development of small businesses and tourism in this country. In its quest for economic renewal, the Government's focus has been and remains the promotion of entrepreneurship.
Mr. Speaker, where the previous Government did nothing but talk to assuage the concerns of small entrepreneurs and developers of tourism facilities, we have taken action. We have recognized the rich potential among our vast community of small entrepreneurs, and we have also adopted rigorous marketing methods for making Canada internationally attractive to tourists.
Mr. Speaker, as my fellow Francophones outside Quebec and my fellow Acadians pointed out upon my appointment to Cabinet, I am the only Francophone outside Quebec sitting in

October 24, 1986
The Address-Mr. Valcourt
the Cabinet. Having grown up as part of a minority group in New Brunswick, I feel I am particularly well-equipped to deal with a difficult task, namely to be responsible for the Native Peoples Economic Development Program.
Mr. Speaker, as you know, our Government is committed to economic autonomy for native peoples, and that forms the basis for my commitment to this program.
The Throne Speech also promises the Government will introduce changes to the Official Languages Act. My goal as a francophone outside Quebec is that the Government, in addition to recognizing language rights in the Act, go one step further to ensure that these rights become a reality in the lives of francophone minorities across this country.
Mr. Speaker, whether we are talking about native peoples economic development programs or the tourist industry or expanding small businesses in this country, our main focus is to promote entrepreneurial values.

The Progressive Conservative Party of Canada has long been the vehicle chosen by independent business entrepreneurs to address their concerns, their needs and their aspirations. For much too long federal policies were implemented without regard to their impact on small business. This Party and this Government have changed that unacceptable situation.
The first Budget of the Government, introduced in the spring of 1985, is widely known as the budget for small business because of the many measures it contained to encourage investment in small business. The 1986 Budget continued along this vein by reducing further the tax burden on small businesses, and by announcing a major incentive to encourage research and development by small business.
We added $1 billion to the amount available for loan guarantees under the Small Businesses Loans Act and we have extended the small business bond program to the end of 1987.
More important, however, the Government has moved to create a better economic climate for the growth of small business. Interest rates, which are of such concern to small businesses, are at their lowest level in years. The climate of confidence has led to increased investment in Canada, has benefited, and will continue to benefit small business operators across the country. In addition, the Government is increasing the amount of government purchasing of goods and services directed to small businesses.

Mr. Speaker, the Speech from the Throne delivered by the Governor General on October 1 attests to our lasting commitment with respect to small business.
Reflecting the achievements of our Government since the election, the Speech from the Throne proposes a fairer and simpler tax system more finely atuned to our economic environment. Our Government is considering new initiatives to strengthen the competitiveness of our businesses; it wants to
remove obstacles to economic growth by reducing the burden of paperwork and regulation; it will press for the removal of barriers to interprovincial trade; and it will introduce programs to promote small business and entrepreneurial values. To this end, it will take measures to improve procurement procedures, to strengthen unsolicited proposals, and make it easier for small business to have access to the technology of Government laboratories.
Mr. Speaker, intent as we are on promoting the entrepreneurial spirit, we must be careful not to smother it. We must keep in mind that our entrepreneurs do take risks, they work long hours, they are at once owners, executive directors, marketing experts and accountants, and because of these many responsibilities they always have hard decisions to make.
I am sure Hon. Members will agree that it is difficult enough for an entrepreneur to launch a new business and make it prosper without having to cope with interference from governments at various levels.
Mr. Speaker, this is why, having recognized these facts, our Government identified the need to reduce red tape and to ensure that Government regulations become a tool to help businesses rather than to hinder their growth.
My predecessor, the Hon. Andre Bissonnette, initiated a federal-provincial survey of the bureaucratic problems which hinder the small business sector. Over 1,100 small businessmen throughout the country were also asked for their views on this question: Who in their opinion impeded their efforts to expand their business?
Mr. Speaker, I shall be meeting with my provincial colleagues next week to assess the results of this survey, and I can assure the House that our Government will develop an action plan to attack squarely the obstacle to entrepreneurship posed by red tape.
We shall improve further our procurement methods which I have already mentioned by formulating a policy for the efficient promotion of subcontracting to small businesses in both the public and private sectors. The Small Business Secretariat is sponsoring a debate on subcontracting in the private sector at the Small Businesses Show which I inaugurated this morning in Montreal. The forum provided by our Department at the show will allow small and large businessmen to exchange ideas on how subcontracting can promote and enhance small businesses while benefiting larger companies.
We are also on the point of completing a major study to determine to what extent small and large businesses can cooperate in the development and transfer of new technologies through business associations. This is something which we intend to pursue because we are convinced that it could provide a means to improve the competitiveness of small businesses.
As a Member from New Brunswick and more especially the Madawaska-Victoria constituency, Mr. Speaker, I cannot
October 24, 1986

outline my action plan as Minister for Small Businesses and Tourism without first commenting briefly on a vital issue for Atlantic Canada and New Brunswick, as well as for many other regions throughout the country. Mr. Speaker, I am referring to regional development.
The Throne Speech clearly shows this Government's commitment to meeting the challenge of reducing regional inequalities, and in a novel way. This Government's approach, which the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) referred to in his speech in this debate, is aimed at recognizing entrepreneurship as the way to salvation.
Development policies of the past have failed miserably. We believe the development policies that work are based on the potential of local entrepreneurs. Also, the time has come to recognize the need to coordinate Government efforts and harmonize them with the initiatives of entrepreneurs on the regional level.
Mr. Speaker, that process reflects this Government's new approach and Prime Minister Mulroney's commitment to regional development and to the citizens of Atlantic Canada.
Our objective for reducing disparities in Atlantic Canada and elsewhere, for instance for diversifying the Western economy, necessarily entails the development of small businesses. The latter are a key component of this objective and we must spare no effort to reach that objective.
I would now like to comment in a somewhat more detailed way on the means 1 propose to recommend to the Government, first to help promote Canada's small businesses. Second to fully exploit the tourist potential of our great country, and finally to support native self-sufficiency.
Mr. Speaker, only since this Government was elected has the potential of our tourist industry been recognized in the Canadian economy. Only since this Government was elected has support been forthcoming for the efforts made by our resort operators who are attempting to put this country on the international map by promoting Canada as a tourist destination area. Mr. Speaker, 1986 will have been an excellent year for tourism in Canada, and by far. More than two million tourists visited our country during the first eight months of 1986. This means our tourist trade deficit has decreased 92 per cent, with gains of more than $200 million for the Canadian economy. That remarkable recovery was obtained because of the ability and leadership of my predecessors in this function. They turned Tourism Canada towards foreign markets and established a new relationship with the tourist industry, the Provinces and the Territories. Such a success is also due to Expo '86, which we have supported financially, and also to the organizers of Expo '86, the British Columbia Government and, of course, the City of Vancouver.
Thanks to them, this year, that world exposition brought a great many visitors to Canada. I must also recognize, however, that another factor explains the record number of tourists who came to Canada this year. I refer to the marketing effort directed at the United States by our department on the theme Canada, the World Next Door. An assessment, of this new marketing approach, Mr. Speaker, has revealed that this campaign has made Americans much more aware and
The Address-Mr. Valcourt
informed concerning Canada as a tourist destination and that, thanks to this awareness, they were much more eager to come here. The importance of the tourist industry in Canada demands an aggressive approach focussed on our successes. A great many people do not seem to realize that the tourist industry in Canada contributes $20 billion to the Canadian economy and accounts for over 600,000 jobs for Canadian men and women. Well, we have to build on this resource.
To achieve this, I intend to continue working closely with our partners in industry and our provincial colleagues to ensure that our joint tourism efforts remain co-ordinated, stable and representative of the needs of the industry. I will also continue our focused marketing effort on the international front, particularly in the United States where our biggest market lies within a day's drive from our border. Next year, with Expo 86 over and the Calgary Olympics a year away, we must be even more aggressive in promoting Canada in our key foreign markets.
While 1986 was a great year for tourism in Canada, the benefits of this year were not felt evenly across the country. I will, therefore, be examining ways to spread these benefits more broadly in all regions of the country. I believe now is the time to have more regionally-sensitive marketing campaigns which will show off all regions of the country through specific products grouping. This will, of course, come under our major umbrella marketing campaign.
We will continue to explore new ways to market Canada abroad through our partners in industry under joint cost-shared efforts. We will continue to manage the tourism subagreements with the provinces in the fields of product development, marketing and planning, thereby ensuring top-notch tourism facilities across the country. Tourism can be a strong regional development tool. It seeks to promote the best Canada has to offer in terms of culture, hospitality, leisure activities and scenery.

Mr. Speaker, I should like now to advise you and other Hon. Members of what we intend to do concerning small businesses. My first and foremost priority will be of course to assume fully all my responsibilities as defender of, promoter of, and spokesman for small businessmen in this country. I shall assume these responsibilities by working in close co-operation with my Cabinet colleagues who will strive to implement the various measures announced in the Throne Speech. All Hon. Members will agree, Mr. Speaker, that the forthcoming debate on the tax reform announced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) will affect directly all small businesses in Canada. The Minister of Finance with whom I have discussed this issue is very well aware already of the needs and concerns of small businessmen in this area of utmost importance. I intend to consult with him frequently and, as the reform process is progressing, to submit to him the options most likely to benefit small Canadian businessmen.

October 24, 1986
The Address-Mr. Valcourt
As I have already indicated, we will table soon a detailed action plan to solve the problem which heavy paperwork is creating for small businesses. The plan will deal more specifically with the needless duplication of forms.

We must also take steps to improve delivery of financial assistance programs to small businesses. This means simpler application forms, reduced bureaucratic red tape, particularly for lower levels of assistance, and faster turnaround of each application. We will continue to find ways to meet the financial needs of small businesses across Canada. Existing financial mechanisms will be assessed for their ability to provide adequate debt equity and venture financing to small businesses. In particular, we must look at the financial needs of our smallest small businesses and find new ways to anchor equity investment in their start-up and future expansion.

One of the most important contributions of the small business community is related to industrial innovation. Entrepreneurs are by definition innovators. It rests with the Government to see that its policies promote that role.
With respect to another program for which I am responsible, the economic development of native people, we will have to carry on along the same lines despite the fact that some people will claim the results are not very sensitive.
I agree that much work remains to be done in the efforts to promote economic self-reliance among our native populations. By necessity, that work must begin with existing native economic development programs. Therefore, I am considering measures to improve the delivery of the Native Economic Development Program, to expand the eligibility criteria associated with the program and to ensure a greater regional balance in its efforts by encouraging more projects from the North and from the Atlantic region. Each of these improvements has resulted, and will continue to result, from close consultation with native leaders and with the Native Economic Development Board itself.
Why do we attach so much importance to small business? Because small business is responsible for 70 per cent of the new jobs that are created. It is largely in small business that the spirit of Canadian entrepreneurship manifests itself. Indeed, the dynamism of our entrepreneurs has now become the main source of employment and economic growth in Canada.
Another important aspect is that women entrepreneurs, who are playing increasingly important roles in our economy now, own one out of three small businesses, up from 18 per cent a decade ago. Studies also show that the success of female-owned small business is almost double that of their maleowned counterparts. The Government will do everything possible to create an environment in which these businesswomen can create jobs.

Similar efforts will also be made to encourage our young people to contribute to the prosperity of our country by instilling into them that spirit of entrepreneurship and by providing them with that institutional framework which without restricting their independence and their creativity will still allow them to see their dreams come true.

Mr. Speaker, I seek the Minister's comments with respect to the Canada-Alberta tourism subagreement. I speak for southern Alberta when I make this comment. As the Minister knows, although in a sense it was before his time in public life, relations between the federal Government and the provincial Governments were at an all-time low. I suspect that one of the major reasons he became involved in politics was because of this. However, as a result of the Progressive Conservative Government coming into office with the feeling that federal-provincial relations were at an all-time low we have now signed, I believe, over 50 economic regional development agreements in the Province of Alberta. One such agreement was a tourism subagreement. I want to tell the Minister just how well that agreement is working.
As the Hon. Member for Lethbridge-Foothills it is an absolute delight to attend meetings at which there are tourism officials from the City of Lethbridge, a city of about 60,000 people, and officials from the surrounding towns and villages, including Waterton Lakes National Park. It is a pleasure to watch these people finally come together under the auspices of this tourism subagreement. They now look at southern Alberta as a whole as opposed to the City of Lethbridge competing with the Town of Cardston or Crowsnest for these tourists. They are now coming together to develop plans by which people can make a circle tour and spend a day or two in all parts of southern Alberta. This is an absolute delight to watch, and it would not have occurred without the tourism subagreement.
The tourism subagreement has permitted people with all sorts of good ideas and energy to come forward with innovative projects and make applications for up to 35 per cent capital contribution from the tourism subagreement. As a result some very innovative projects have been approved in my riding. I know that this is happening in other parts of Alberta as well. On behalf of the people who come to me involved in this tourism subagreement, whether they be tourist officers, motel owners or small business people, I wish to thank the Minister. I wish to express to the Minister their appreciation for this approach.
October 24, 1986

1 would now like to ask a question of the Minister. Can the Minister tell us how many other provinces have these tourism subagreements? If the other provinces do not have such agreements, then I would strongly urge the Minister to press them for this type of agreement since it works quite well.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with great pleasure that I rise in the House today to give you my comments on the Speech from the Throne.
Mr. Speaker, my first comment concerns the order in which the various issues were approached by the Government in the Throne Speech.
The Conservative Government started with national reconciliation, followed by economic renewal, constructive internationalism and, finally, social justice.
Mr. Speaker, with respect, I doubt that Canadian men and women are more concerned about Canada's international role than they are about social justice. In fact, many polls have clearly indicated that the main concerns of the Canadian people are unemployment and social needs. I am afraid, however, that the rank given social justice in the Throne Speech is an accurate reflection of its place on the Conservative Government's priority list, despite the Government's flowing rhetoric on the subject.
Where the status of women is concerned, the Conservative Government has announced some intentions that are indeed of interest. In the past, however, statements by this Government have seldom been translated into concrete action. It would seem this time will be no exception.
I am delighted that the Government has at last recognized the need for adjusting to structural changes in the family unit. Indeed, only about 15 per cent of our families consist of a husband who works while the wife stays home. If we look at the structure of our families today, we must not forget that a number of years ago, women did not work outside the home and had an average of four children-I am talking about 25 years ago-and if we look at today's birthrate and the profile of the traditional family, we realize that the picture has changed quite a bit. We must remember that the traditional
family, where children are living with their biological parents and the father is the sole breadwinner, accounts for only 10 per cent.
Single-parent families constitute 29 per cent of Canadian households. And according to Statistics Canada's figures as of November 1985, 57.5 per cent of women with preschool children are on the labour market; 67 per cent of women who have paid employment are working full time although they have young children, and the majority of women in their optimum childbearing years are on the labour market. In 1984, 69 per cent of women between the ages of 25 and 34 were on the labour market.
Considering the various roles played by women in our society, I think we should introduce a series of measures aimed at helping couples to cope satisfactorily with the needs of their families. Among these measures, daycare is a priority. Perhaps I may add that the need for daycare centres is recognized in the Speech from the Throne, but instead of announcing specific measures, the Government has simply decided to undertake some vague discussions with the provincial governments, the unions and the private sector. In brief, a lot of rhetoric but little action. Canadian men and women expected much more on child care from this Government, because we are now facing a real crisis. Indeed, there is only room for 9 per cent of our children who need those services in the child care system. People who work there are paid less than zoo attendants.
Mr. Speaker, that situation is totally unacceptable. Thousands of people have testified before the Special Committee on Child Care. Men and women from all across Canada have explained to us their dismay at the difficulties they experience, the enormous problems they are facing to have their children cared for when they have to go to work or attend classes. What the Canadian people need and are now looking for is action, not empty words.
When you see what this Government is doing for pension funds, you ought to look closer into having homemakers covered by pension plans in Canada. That was one of the many promises made by the Conservative Government during the election campaign, and made again last year by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp). The shifting phraseology I noticed in the Throne Speech is worthy of ancient Greek philosophy. In fact, they are now talking about admitting spouses of existing contributors into pension plans rather than all those who look after the household, those who are without a spouse.
This, Mr. Speaker, discriminates against the heads of singleparent families, 72 per cent of whom are women. The most insidious aspect is that once again women are discriminated against, based on whether or not they have a spouse. It seems to me that in 1986, the Government should be ready to change all that.
October 24, 1986

If we take a closer look at the National Council of Welfare report we can see that the poverty rate for the elderly and for men has declined, but unfortunately poverty is getting worse with respect to the condition of women who are single, elderly and heads of families.
I should like to remind the House that, unlike most other groups of Canadians, six out of 10 single-parent families headed by women live under the threshold of poverty. The rate of poverty among single mothers did not go down in 1985, quite the contrary, they have been getting ever poorer over the past five years. Compared with a married woman, a single mother is five times more likely to end up among the poor. Women account for nearly 60 per cent of underprivileged women between ages 16 and 64. Although they make up 51 per cent of the population, seven poor and elderly persons out of 10 are women. These women represent 83 per cent of low income, single and elderly people. Such disparity is even more obvious among single-parent families. A family headed by a woman is four times more likely to be poor than another one headed by a man.
I think this is an altogether discouraging situation and I am somewhat upset to hear the Minister responsible for the Status of Women say that the Conservative Government has done a lot for women. It may be that she has done a lot for women who are fairly well-off or who belong to the middle class, and it would seem that the Government is taking a rather socialistic and elitist approach, because I suggest that Government action with respect to the poor and low-income families has been minimal at best. Not a word in the Speech from the Throne relates to homemakers.
There is also a reference to the number of women appointed recently to the highest levels of the Public Service and to federal boards and commissions. I admit this came as a great surprise to me, because I monitor these appointments very closely, and I would like to know which statistics the Conservative Government was using to be able to make those claims. Personally, I take a different view of the situation, since hardly 20 per cent of the appointees are women.
Another promise made by the Conservative Government concerned part-time work. The Prime Minister spoke very firmly on the subject and said several times that one of his priorities in helping women would be to establish a definition of part-time work and to require employers to provide fringe benefits in proportion to the number of hours worked. Unfortunately, two years later, still not a word, not a single reference to part-time work. Not even in the Throne Speech. We all know that today, many families need that second salary, and in 42 per cent of families with two parents and two children, most women have to work because one salary is not enough to keep them above the poverty line. The Conservative Government had promised to take action in this regard, but there is not a single mention of it in the Speech from the Throne.
The Address-Mrs. Pepin
If we look more closely, we find that there might be legislation to eliminate violent forms of pornography. I trust that this legislation will not suffer the same fate as Bill C-114, which died on the order paper.
Finally, how can we talk about assistance to battered women when the Conservative Government is willing to subsidize only halfway houses and shelters which operate under pilot programs? I was rather surprised to note that the Conservative Government is now saying that it will provide some assistance to shelters for battered women because the excessive cutbacks to this program in the last two years have resulted in the closing of many such shelters.
Last June, a meeting of the national women's groups was held in Ottawa, and the then Secretary of State, Mr. Bouchard, met with their representatives who told him how harmful the cutbacks had been. Naturally, the Minister replied that the Government would take care of everything and that there would be no recurrence of the problem. Recently, we heard about all the women who had to be refused admission to the shelters. In Edmonton, 250 women who had been the victim of family violence had to be turned away because of a lack of space. The same happened in Calgary and it is happening now in the Yukon and in Winnipeg. The Government is now saying: We shall deal with it. I think that it would be more honest for the Government to say that the problem it has created will be corrected because the situation of shelters for battered women is quite disastrous.
The Government also states that the family is the foundation of our society. That is all very well, but I hope that the Government will act on it because, after its two Budgets, we found that a family with two children and an income between $18,000 and $25,000 was paying substantially more taxes than before, which was certainly not the case for families which much higher incomes.
When I look at what the Throne Speech says about women, I have the feeling that it is mostly paying lip service to this issue. We are told that the Government has taken action, that it has done something useful in introducing the Employment Equity Act. Yet, all the groups that appeared before the committee said without exception that the Bill would be totally ineffective because it has no teeth. I only hope that the Government will stop talking and finally take some action to help women. We want to promote women and give them their rightful place in society, but the most important element to consider is the economic position of women. It and its products have been the bargaining ploy that we have put on the table of international negotiation to obtain ends for other interests. In 1954 the imports of horticultural products amounted to $125 million. In 1985, 31 years later, we are now importing $1.1 billion worth of fruits and vegetables as a result of very favourable access for international suppliers in the Canadian market. This is something which must be brought to a halt. We must ask for fair play. We can no longer receive on the Canadian market bottles of wine from foreign countries, particularly from the EEC, at less than the cost of bottling in this country. I use this item because wine only arrives here with a subsidy, and it is the most extreme example that I can give.
However, let us come to the apple industry. We find that in the past we have received apple juice in the Canadian market-a product produced in Canada-at less than the cost of packaging and transportation. It is dumped into this market to the detriment of the Canadian industry.
It is then imperative that Canada seek fair trading opportunity in the world. Whether it applies to agriculture, fish or in whatever product we may trade, our markets in the world must be fair. We are a trading nation. We must seek to achieve world competence, world quality, world productivity and world competitive costs. That must become an objective of Government in leadership and an objective of unions, management, capital and financiers throughout this land. These are our objectives and on this basis we can compete in an international society. We must compete if we are to survive. This must be the tenet upon which all facets of our economy and our Government must base its future negotiations and retain a competitive position within our own market and a competitive capability in those items in which we can be world productive and competent. That has to be our objective. Then and only then can we be a prosperous nation as we should and wish to be.
In the horticultural industry, there are certain seasonal tariffs which are not negotiable as far as that industry is concerned. We have come into production in most of our horticultural crops at that season of the year when the United States of America is just about at the end of its production and is dumping any balance it may have on any market which it can find, and Canada is the handiest market. best. We must then retain an element of protection to retain some strength in that horticultural industry.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity to talk about an aspect of the Throne Speech which I believe has received too little attention. I am referring to a brief paragraph which states: "My Government recognizes that security is the surest safeguard of liberty". It goes on to talk about increasing our NATO contingent in western Europe.
I am one who, against the general weight of feeling within the Christian tradition, was persuaded in World War II to join the Army in order to kill people for the opposition of facism. I have since then wondered very deeply why our country and our allies become engaged in war. I very much regret the one-sided emphasis in those words. I very much regret the exaggerated reliance which that paragraph places on terror, the suggestion that we will have liberty and, for that matter, peace through terror. There was once the Roman Empire. Those of us who studied Caesar will know the motto of the Romans was: "If you want peace, prepare for war". That was good in Julius Caesar's time when he had a growing and expanding empire. But that is long gone. Its power to terrorize its neighbours disappeared when it made its neighbours its slaves and no longer had the power to terrorize them.
I deeply distrust the continuation of the philosophy that we must terrorize whoever it is we think disagrees with us. The previous Prime Minister entertained a similar philosophy when he said: "What we have to do is scare hell out of the Russians". It did not work. The means used to scare hell out of the Russians are scaring hell out of us. I would rather place my reliance not only in the Christian and Jewish tradition, but I believe with the majority of the people of the world, in words such as these: The work of justice shall be peace and the effect of justice, quietness and confidence forever, keep judgment and do justice for my salvation as near to come and my justice to be revealed. In other words, while we struggle with our conflicting actual fears, the hope should be placed not in creating more fear. The hope for peace and liberty has to be placed on the creation of a more just world, not on the creation of more terror.
For that reason, I regret further that there is no warning in the Speech from the Throne against the dangers of militarization. We think of this as a country of peaceful people. Yet our economy and our Government are becoming militarized. By "militarization" I mean mainly the promoting of war-related

enterprises only for profit or income and without serious examination of the danger they pose to life, peace, the economy and even to the environment.
