There is very little public opportunity to examine the facts. There is very little listening to the millions of people in Canada who, in one way or another, have gone on record, and will go on record again this weekend, and who have been going on record daily during this week in Toronto, asking for peace, for an end to the arms race. These are people who hoped that there would be some result at the summit conference in Reykavik two weeks ago. They were disappointed when the President of the United States, our ally, stonewalled all the substantial offers made by the other side by insisting on his absolute right to conduct the crazy scheme of star wars. This Government, under the excuse of restraint, starves unemployment insurance allowances, public day care, health and education expenditures, social housing and even the farming industry, giving too little too late to recognize disasters. The sake of maintaining our industry against subsidized imports, as one of the previous speakers mentioned, this Government starves the manufacturing industry. Perhaps it would like to see it disappear from Canada as has the clothing industry. Only one industry is actively supported by the Government. When the Government brings the shopping team up from the Pentagon and continues subsidizing the export of arms, that is where its heart is, in the high profits, not in defence. It gives critical backing to the terrorist policies of the United States Government in Nicaragua. It gives back-door support to star wars. Of course, those who dare to criticize that enterprise are often accused of having doubtful loyalty to Canada without any basis for the accusation.
A principal example which has come to my attention in the last few months is the Canadian Forces Base at Goose Bay, with the training in low-level flying under contract for NATO Governments, to the great distress and harm to the life of the native people in that area. For some years there has been a program of training pilots to fly low over the hills of Labrador. This is not for sport, of course, although they tend to make it a sport. They seem to like to scare the caribou herds, which can be fatal to caribou cows when they are calfing. They seem to like to scare the Indian and Inuit families when they are hunting, as they have done for thousands of years before we

October 24, 1986
The Address-Mr. Heap
interrupted them. They seem to like to pollute the air and lake waters with the exhaust of their low flying aircraft. The excuse is, of course, to train pilots to fly low over the hills of Eastern Europe and into the Soviet Union under its radar. In other words, this is to provide for a policy which the Americans sometimes call "deep strike" but which in fact amounts to "first strike".
The native people of this area for years have struggled with the Government over their land claims, that they should be able to exercise their right over the land as they did for a long time. Nevertheless, the Government has stonewalled them, and even when a vast iron ore deposit was opened up, little was done to ensure that it was a means of livelihood for the people who had lived there for so long. In fact, the company which was operating the iron ore mining in one part of Labrador decided to close it down shortly before the Canadian President of that American subsidiary decided to go into politics to become the Prime Minister of Canada. Now that those people have been deprived of that livelihood, they are being pressured into becoming hewers of wood and drawers of waters, or perhaps becoming servants in the cafeteria on a NATO base which the Government is willing to attract to Labrador by spending perhaps $100 million of taxpayers' money.
Our Government, and the people of Canada, have an obligation to respect all the cultures of our country, not only the French and the English, the Italian, the Chinese, the Ukrainian and others who have come here, but also that of the peoples who were here for thousands of years before our ancestors arrived. A year ago the Government heard briefs at a short committee hearing in Yellowknife from representatives of the Dene Nation and the Metis association in which they called for a defence policy and foreign policy of non-alignment. These people have, for many generations and centuries, tried to live in such a way as not to threaten their neighbours and not to pollute and destroy the land on which they live. They do not eagerly tie themselves to a boom and bust economy of competition and war. We should be listening to their wisdom and considering the question they ask. Is it really necessary for Canada to follow one of these two armed giants in the world?
Another committee of Parliament listened to a similar representation from a group which spoke on the matter of Goose Bay. The Standing Committee on Environment and Forestry in its report tabled in Parliament at the end of June addressed a motion to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Beatty) which stated that he should immediately halt all north shore and Labrador low-level military air flights and assess the effects of such flights on the environment in these regions as soon as possible. The committee, made up of course by a large majority of government Members, studied the protests of the native peoples against the pollution and the disruption of their lives caused by the low-flying planes. This was the direction the committee gave to the Minister of National Defence.
I think that the 120 days which he has to respond to the committee have just about expired. I hope he will soon tell us whether he respects the advice of the committee and the plea of the people in that area. By this motion the committee is defending Canadians, defending Canada's land, by asking the Minister to halt the flights now and to investigate.
The Government of Quebec is taking a similar stand. The Government of Quebec will not leave it to the slow-moving investigation to be undertaken finally by Cabinet. It will add its own investigation, too, since it is not only Labrador that is threatened by this low-flying program but also certain parts of Quebec. Church leaders in the Goose Bay area, and other areas, have publicly questioned who it is that will benefit from the half a billion dollars or more that would be spent on the NATO base and whether, in a starving world, it is right to waste so much money on armaments.
Of course, the argument of the Minister of National Defence and the military is that they believe they are defending Canada. But that is exactly the claim that many Canadians are calling into question. In the case of the base at Goose Bay, the pilots who will be trained to fly over the hills of eastern Europe and into the Soviet Union give the Soviet Union good reason to fear a first strike. It is common knowledge that if one believes in the effectiveness of the fear of first strike, then the response to that fear is to strike first. In other words, if we believe that the Soviet Union is willing to attack our country, then the danger of bringing that attack much sooner than we expect is increased by the provocative and threatening plan called deep strike, and by the training of our pilots for carrying out such a plan. This is of a piece with the Pershing and Cruise missiles in Europe which are 10 or 12 minutes' flight away from Moscow, or whatever it is, depending on where they are based.
We have no such threat against us in North America. It is not easy to imagine what it is like to live in a country that has already within living memory been twice invaded by the armies of the West, once by what we called the Allies and once by a country we called the enemy but which was partly armed for that purpose by corporations, especially American ones. It is now threatened with the destruction of its major cities in a matter of minutes. There is no sign that the citizens of that country are being intimidated into surrendering their country. They have made an extraordinary move of unilateral nuclear disarmament. That is the only name that can be put on the moratorium on testing, since the United States claims that to stop testing would weaken it militarilly, to quote the words of President Reagan. The Soviet Union has been willing to accept a one-year cessation of its nuclear testing in order to invite the United States and its allies, such as Canada, to reach an agreement to end the testing altogether. There is no mention of this in the Speech from the Throne, which I think is unfortunate.
This is a debate which is being carried on in city after city in Canada, not only by people in their living rooms, by people in churches and other public places, but by members of city and
October 24, 1986

municipal councils. It is a debate that will be entertained by the Ontario Legislature within the next few weeks. It will entertain a motion to make Ontario a nuclear weapons free zone. Granted, a motion such as that was passed a few years ago in Toronto City Council, and in many other cities, which does not by itself bring about the goal that it states. However, it registers a strong, wide consensus of the people who believe that we do not get peace or liberty by terrorizing people on the other side of the world or on the other side of the border. If we find a threat which we agree among ourselves must be met, then let us use the means to meet it, as we did in World War II. But let us not continue piling up armaments endlessly in the foolish belief that somehow or other we will terrify the whole world into doing every little thing that President Reagan would like it to do. The belief that every country should turn its Government inside out to suit the President of the United States is an insane belief. It is worrisome that such a person should be the President of the largest country in the world. Canada must disconnect itself from that craziness. We can begin to do that by saying that there will be no NATO base at Goose Bay and no more low-level flying training at Goose Bay.

What kind of public demonstrations has the Hon. Member, a person who is deeply interested in these issues, seen in Canada in the past year? What would he recommend that Members of the House and people across Canada who are concerned with this militarization involve themselves in?

Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague for the question although I will not be able to do justice to it in four minutes. I would mention three actions without trying to deal with all of them.
On Saturday, from Vancouver to St. John's, many of us will engage in a public walk calling for an end to the nuclear arms race. This is an old subject. Many of us were doing the same thing 40 years ago. We have not met our objective yet but there are a great many more people with widely differing political points of view who agree that we have to put an end to the arms race.
Second, I believe we should look to ways to build up our economy and to restore the growth of industries which manufacture goods for peaceful use. 1 am not ashamed to mention the clothing industry as being one which is important to the riding of Spadina. We must do this so that we do not become dependent on the export of arms for a significant part of our national revenue and so that we do not participate in the export of arms to countries which will see, directly or indirectly, that they are used for the suppression of human rights in

October 24, 1986
The Address-Mr. Corbett
places like Latin America, Africa and the western Pacific islands.
Third, I believe we should address our own fears by meeting with the people we fear like the people of the Soviet Union. We should all sit down, not only the two top men, to speak with each other. We should make much more use of the opportunity that exists in the Circumpolar Conference, a conference of the countries around the world that border the Arctic. Those three actions are the kinds of actions I would like to see Parliament discuss as ways of creating peace through justice and through the discussion of a just settlement between us and those we fear.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to be able to participate in the debate on the latest Speech from the Throne. Certainly Canada is in such a state now that economic revival and renewal is something we all eagerly anticipate. 1 was extremely encouraged by several of the remarks that were made in the Speech from the Throne and would anticipate that indeed the serious issues of the day will be addressed.
The Speech from the Throne outlined the Government's three-part strategy designed to promote economic renewal through fiscal responsibility, the removal of obstacles to growth and the encouragement of new investment. We know that the initiative has been taken over the past two years since the election of the Progressive Conservative Government and we know that that initiative has been successful to a certain degree. Indeed, we have seen growth.
Approximately 24,478 new jobs have been created each month since the election of the Progressive Conservative Government. We have seen the Bank of Canada rate fall. We have heard the Conference Board of Canada state that consumer confidence is at its highest level in some 21 years and is at its second highest level on record. The inflation rate has remained pretty well stable at the 4 per cent range for the past two years and we are in the most stable price environment since 1971.
Coming from Atlantic Canada and the constituency of Fundy-Royal, I am no stranger to economic and regional disparity. It was of some concern to us before the Speech from the Throne that this Government perhaps had not moved in distinct enough fashions and ways to address those regional disparities. All of us from the Atlantic region were very pleased to see that the problems of regional disparity were clearly acknowledged in the Speech from the Throne. I believe it is high time that this Government, and most people, acknowledge that inequity is not acceptable to Atlantic Canadians, who generally come from a root stock of proud and self-reliant people determined to play a full and active role in Canada's national life and in this Confederation. Atlantic Canadians are not in the business of looking for more handouts. The fact of the matter is that we want to work our way out of the situation where we have such a significant and substantial dependence on others in this nation to assist us. We
must recognize that Atlantic Canada accepts from the federal Government something in excess of $9 billion more annually than it pays out. That sort of inequity is not justifiable.
There have been several initiatives taken by the Government to facilitate enduring economic development in the region, such as the Atlantic Enterprise Program which will provide $1 billion in loan guarantees; the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Program to promote and encourage government procurement by local firms; Enterprise Cape Breton; and economic and regional development agreements that have been in place now and have demonstrated some sense of success. The agency set up by Atlantic Canada Opportunities will co-ordinate all federal development initiatives in the area. It will have its roots in Atlantic Canada. It will tap the resources and ideas of Atlantic Canadians who will have a direct hand in the operation, policy, and program of development.
We have seen in recent days, and heard in recent hours, of other initiatives and programs that have been put into place. We heard today the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism (Mr. Valcourt) talking about the virtues of small business and how they must be encouraged to establish in Atlantic Canada. In recent weeks, we have heard the Minister of State for Forestry and Mines (Mr. Merrithew) from Saint John declare that the Port of Saint John has been given local port status. This will be a tremendous boon to the Port of Saint John and to New Brunswick as a whole.
More must be done. There is no question that the right steps have been initiated and the right steps have been taken. Atlantic Canada must realize more from this Government than we have ever realized from any of the previous Governments or administrations. Atlantic Canada is in a state of economic decline. It has been in this state of economic decline ever since the national policy was announced in 1879 when there was a determination by the then Government of the day to redirect the normal trade routes from north to south and concentrate in an east to west direction. This was harmful to Atlantic Canada. It was harmful to the maritime provinces, as they were known at that time. Atlantic Canadians and maritimers had been traditionally north-south traders. That hurt us economically, and we have never come back to that time when we did enjoy economic prosperity in concert and equally with the rest of our neighbours to the west.
I believe it is high time that we recognized that there has to be a special relationship between Canada and Atlantic Canada, and recognize the special status that Atlantic Canada has played in the past in the development and creation of this nation.
Mr. Speaker, I am suggesting to you that at this time in our negotiations with the United States when probably the future of the nation, let alone of Atlantic Canada, has never come more into prominence than it has today, that Atlantic Canadians be accorded that special status and recognition which I am calling for.
October 24, 1986

The New England states represent a market with which the maritime provinces are associated and, geographically speaking, we are a natural part of the New England states. It has a population of something in excess of 48 million people. It has a market potential that is twice the size of the entire nation of Canada. Maritimers have had a long historic relationship with the Boston states. We refer to the Boston states with almost a kindred spirit. We look to them as a friendly neighbour and a part of our Atlantic Canadian heritage. It is natural that it should be an area of special consideration, and economic ties between the two should be considered. This is nothing that is new. Back in the 1880s a maritime partner sister of Nova Scotia considered leaving Confederation when it perceived that the union of the provinces and Ottawa had failed to deliver on the promised economic benefits of union and the establishment of Canada.
The coastal states represent the largest market for Atlantic goods. It is a market that has been steadily growing. Our net exports in Atlantic Canada are more than we import. Atlantic Canadians have historically supported a freer trade relationship with New England. I perceive, now that we are involved in these talks, that there is a renewed interest in the Atlantic region and in the concept of a federal regional economic development. We have now seen two decades of policies and programs that have been directed towards developing Atlantic Canada which have not been very effective, to say the least. It is time now that we looked at new avenues of restoring economic confidence in Atlantic Canada.
Many are wondering if stronger economic ties to New England might offer a different type of development and opportunity which may work. As a maritimer and an Atlantic Canadian, I am convinced that more open access to the New England market would bring benefits to our region. Our major exports of fish and forest products could be expected to increase both in output and in level of processing.
We have been hurt by the recent imposition of tariffs and taxes on lumber products. That is just an indication of why it is more important at this stage in our development that indeed we do secure our future by realizing an enhanced trade agreement with the United States. It is particularly important to Atlantic Canadians. If we are successful, that will reduce the uncertainty and difficulties in the present countervailing American duty legislation. Companies in Atlantic Canada have been subjected to commerce investigations to determine if they have been hurt by U.S. companies. This is a very expensive process indeed. We want to be finished with that so we can secure our markets and ensure a future for our people.
If the huge northeastern United States market was opened up to Canadian producers and manufacturers, some of them might be induced to locate in the maritime provinces to manufacture their products for export into the U.S. I call upon the Canadian Government to recognize in its negotiations with the United States the special situation and status of Atlantic
The Address-Mr. Corbett
Canada and to bear that in mind when it is concluding its negotiations with our American neighbours.
I should like to deal with the shipbuilding industry, an extremely important matter to those of us living in Atlantic Canada. I draw the attention of the House to a statement which was made by the Progressive Conservative Party on August 2, 1984. In part it indicated that we must work to meet a greater share of our domestic requirements for vessels used in defence, coastal trade, search and rescue patrol, and the offshore fishery. Also it indicated that a top priority of a Conservative Government would be to create a more viable and prosperous shipbuilding industry and that proposals would be submitted during the consultative process. At that time there were some seven or eight recommendations which we would implement if and when we became the Government of Canada.
The shipbuilding industry in the nation, let alone in Atlantic Canada, is in extremely serious economic difficulty. Unfortunately I have not seen much in the way of movement on the part of the Government to implement any of the policies about which we talked prior to the 1984 election. 1 would suggest that we move to implement some of the programs about which we talked.
Also I draw to the attention of the House a statement by the Canadian Shipbuilding and Ship Repair Association which directed its thoughts toward four of the policies which we noted at that time-to impose a moratorium on ship imports for domestic use, to introduce concessionary financing for Canadian domestic ships, to apply a 25 per cent tariff on fishing vessels over 100 feet, and to accelerate the naval programs and the Polar 8 ice-breaker program. I support and endorse those recommendations of the Canadian shipbuilding industry. I call upon the Government which I support to implement those policies which we said we would implement prior to the 1984 election. It is high time that we recognized the contribution which the shipbuilding industry has made and can make to the nation. We recognize that that industry is in a state of decline and that merchant fleets are overwhelmed with excess tonnage.
The Saint John Shipbuilding Company is comprised of a group of people with tremendous vision and foresight. It has now put together a team of experts in the field of naval construction and has determined that it will specialize in this direction. I applaud the initiative and foresight of that company. If it is to succeed, as I am sure it will, it must direct its attention to more specialized fields. With the type of infrastructure currently in place, there can be no doubt that a significant amount of naval contracts, whether they be for frigates or submarines, should go to shipyards in Atlantic Canada, particularly that shipyard in New Brunswick which has focused its attention on that particular sector.
I note as well that the Saint John yard is one of the three yards being considered by a consortium looking at the construction of the Polar 8 ice-breaker as being the logical place for it. I call upon the Government to give high priority to
734

October 24, 1986
The Address-Mr. Corbett
the yard located in the City of Saint John when the contract for the Polar 8 super ice-breaker is let.
My final point concerns the policies announced by the Minister responsible for Parks Canada. 1 am delighted that we will look at a new parks policy. Fundy National Park is in my constituency. In the opinion of many people-and it is mine as well-it is one of the most beautiful parks in the Dominion of Canada. I ask that serious attention be paid to that park. There are several areas which we could improve. There are also several things to which the Minister can respond. They have been brought to his attention by the people of Alma and other nearby villages. Some of the suggestions were to reinstate the interpretative walks, to hire a recreational director and staff, to construct a visitors' centre with a marine display and a tidal viewing stand, to extend the golf course by 18 holes, to update the Highlands Inn to resource status, to restore the Alma mill site, and to construct the maple sugar grove. Fundy National Park is the nearest national park in the entire nation to the American border. It is only realistic that it should be developed with special attention and with special care.
I applaud the Minister for his visit to the region last spring. The people were delighted that for the first time since the park was inaugurated in the 1950s a Minister responsible for Parks Canada had the interest to visit Fundy National Park, our little region of the country, to talk with them, to hear their concerns firsthand, and to witness the beauty of the region.
The process for economic development has been started by the Government. I look forward to serving with it over the next two years in a very positive and constructive way. I wish us the best in developing the political will to implement the policies we have started.

Mr. Speaker, I spent part of my summer vacation in the Fundy National Park of which the Hon. Member for Fundy Royal (Mr. Corbett) spoke so highly. Indeed it is a very fine part of the country. I have two questions for the Hon. Member.
Has it not been a source of disappointment to him to have had so little definition and direction given to the much heralded Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency announced in the Throne Speech? This is the end of the Throne Speech debate. I hoped that by now there would be at least some sense of what exactly the agency is to do. Does the Hon. Member share my sense of disappointment that the agency is still some kind of pie in the sky solution to Atlantic Canadian problems without being defined in any sense?
Based upon some discussions with those involved in the free trade negotiations with the United States, does it seem likely that it is necessary for us to give up in order to attain certain objectives for which the Conservative Government is looking in its free trade talks? Does it seem necessary to give up the regional support packages which were so much a part of the country's commitment to Atlantic Canada and to other parts of the country? If we seem likely to have to sacrifice that, as is
my view of what is likely, will this change the Member's view of what is so advantageous with respect to the potential of free trade arrangements between Canada and the United States?

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to congratulate the Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor (Mr. Langdon) on his good judgment in choosing Fundy National Park for part of his summer vacation. I am saddened that he had not contacted me while in the area because I could have introduced him to a number of interesting aspects of the park, to some local people, to the local heritage and the history of the area in which I am sure he would have taken a great deal of interest. Perhaps he will think about coming back to Fundy National Park in the future. With the Minister's new proposals and his interest in parks across the nation, Fundy as well as other parks will be the beneficiary of those programs.
As far as the Atlantic Enterprise Program and the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Program are concerned, it must be recognized that these are mammoth undertakings upon which the Government has embarked. Let me draw to the Hon. Member's attention that just last year the IRD Program alone committed something like $88 million to small business promotion in New Brunswick. I am not sure what the total figure is for Atlantic Canada, but that is a significant amount of money for the Province of New Brunswick alone. The billion dollars to which the Atlantic Enterprise Program has committed itself in guaranteeing loans to small businesses is probably one of the most substantial moves that I have witnessed. If the Hon. Member knows of any other program by previous administrations, I invite him to draw it to our attention. I do not think that that can be the case. Nevertheless, the Atlantic [DOT]Enterprise Program is one of the most exciting programs and one of vision, that I have witnessed in my experience as a Member of Parliament. These programs, just by nature of their size and complexity, are naturally taking some time to implement. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) in Moncton a few days ago has lowered the ceiling for eligibility to apply for that program from $200,000 to $100,000. We were very pleased about that. Despite the fact that there have been some hitches, some natural problems that you would expect in dealing with a program of this size, the fact is that the program is in place. It is moving ahead and people will and are taking advantage of it. I am certainly very enthusiastic about its prospects.
The freer trade issue to which the Hon. Member refers cannot help but benefit Atlantic Canadians. I believe that along the way there will be casualties, but there will be more winners than losers and the winners will be winning big. The casualties will probably be casualties at any rate. These casualties will be the people located in Atlantic Canada who are finding it very, very difficult to compete in industry and in manufacturing in Canada just because of their distance from markets and difficulties in establishing their industries at arm's length from where they have an opportunity to sell their products.
October 24, 1986

Being an Atlantic Canadian I know that with our historic ties, the opportunities we have had in the past, our natural heritage and the fact that so many people go back and forth to the New England States-the Boston States as we refer to them-the impact will be substantial. If there is to be criticism about our trade negotiations it cannot be criticism for trying. I should think that the only criticism that one should get would be for not trying. We should not be criticized for trying. If we are the winners, I suggest to the Hon. Member that Atlantic Canada will be as big a winner if not the biggest winner in the entire nation.

speechtext: Resuming debate. The Hon. Member for Mount Royal (Mrs. Finestone).

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a Throne Speech is an interesting reflection of the social and political philosophies of a Government. We learn a great deal about its political program and agenda and what it does or does not stand for. This past year in its Throne Speech the Government returned to the 19th century, the social Darwinism theories of survival of the fittest. That is where the Government seems content to remain. The Government takes away from the poor and the powerless and gives to the rich and strong. We agree that the deficit must be addressed, a deficit that grew because of its great safety net which supported our citizens during the severe recession of the early 1980s. We also agree that action must be taken, but not on the backs of the elderly, the sick, the one-parent families or the middle-aged unemployed, those who are least able to bear the burden.
This Government seems unable to act in a consistent fashion. We are told by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) that the country is almost bankrupt, that government spending must be reduced, that transfer payments to the provinces must be cut because the federal deficit must decline. But at the same time, the Prime Minister finds $1 billion to save the uninsured depositors of the Western Bank disaster. He found
The Address-Mrs. Finestone
another $600 million to assist in the purchase of Gulf Canada, and yet another $56 million to change the colour of our soldiers' uniforms. He just recently decided to spend $41 million on a maximum security prison in his riding, the wrong type in the wrong place. This is a first-class boondoggle.
The media has said that the Throne Speech contains something for everyone, that it tries to be all things to all people. Well, I disagree. All that is demonstrated is the Government's lack of political will to close the widening gap between the rich and the poor. It contains an unfair, uneven approach to responsible Government. The Government continues to practise the favouring of the well-to-do by increasing capital gains allowances and RRSPs to levels that the majority of Canadians cannot even dream of while it continues to deindex family allowance and the income tax table a sneaky hidden 3 per cent per year.
Not only am I concerned about the social and economic well being of the people in this country, I am interested as well in the country's growth as an independent, sovereign political entity with all its indigenous richness of heritage and culture.
Under Liberal leadership in the 1970s, the arts in Canada enjoyed a growth rate of which there were few equals in the economy. At the start of the decade there were five professional dance companies in Canada. By 1980 there were 23. The number of professional theatres increased sixfold to 121 and half of their productions were Canadian. The number of professional visual artists more than doubled to 28,755, while the number of publishing houses had more than doubled to 89, almost three-quarters of them now Canadian-owned.
I could tell you about what happened in theatre, dance, symphony orchestras. Elowever, the point that I would like to make is that Pierre Berton, appearing before the Senate Committee on Mass Media in 1970, said that we must sing our own songs and dream our own dreams. It was with this in mind that Canadian artists began to repatriate themselves to Canada and they won major victories.
Canadian content requirements for TV and radio, in the latter instance creating a foundation for a Canadian pop music industry, the withdrawal of tax privileges from foreign magazines, the disallowance for tax purposes of commercials placed by Canadian companies on U.S. border TV stations and, by far the most important of all, the increase in spending on culture by all Governments, which reached more than $2 billion by the early 1980s, was very important. The Liberal Government was a Government of vision promoting pride in our Canadian heritage.
I wish to comment upon the specific language used by the Government in the second to last page of the Throne Speech. I cannot refer you to the particular page number because the Government has omitted to place any page numbers on the copies of the Throne Speech which it distributed.

October 24, 1986
The Address
In the first paragraph of the second to last page of the Throne Speech it is stated:
-we must ensure that all Canadians can pursue their own dreams and expand their own opportunities through greater use of information and knowledge about one another and the world beyond.
I wonder how Canadians are able to "pursue their own dreams" when they do not see images of themselves reflected on their own broadcast media.
For instance, the Caplan-Sauvageau Report on broadcasting concluded quite correctly that there is too little drama programming available on our TV sets. Only 2 per cent of the drama programs seen on English-language TV in this country is Canadian in origin. Furthermore, only 28 per cent of all programming hours available in this country in the English language is Canadian in content. English Canadians, in other words, are virtual strangers in television's land of the imagination. When the Throne Speech refers to expanding information and knowledge about the world beyond, I say that we would like to learn of the world including areas beyond the United States.
On French-language TV 57 per cent of the programs available are Canadian, but the actual viewing of Canadian shows exceeds the proportion of available French-language programming. According to the Caplan-Sauvageau Report this demonstrates that Canadians do watch Canadian content programs. In fact, according to that report the amount of Canadian programs which are watched by our viewers is directly proportional to the amount available. In other words, the more Canadian programs are available in the English and French languages, the more Canadians are likely to watch.
We do not need the Caplan-Sauvageau Report to tell us that there is a chronic shortage of quality Canadian TV programs for our children. The report does tell us, however, that the production of children's French-language and English-language TV programs at CBC Radio Canada is declining because of budget cut-backs imposed by the Government on the CBC. This leaves our children to watch American cartoons which exhibit a tendency for strident, often violent, action. How can the Government continue to play politics with the minds of our children? This issue is too important to be left to partisan politics. Therefore, I had hoped there would be some indication in the Throne Speech that the Government would work with both opposition Parties to increase Canadian content programming for our children as well as Canadian programming in general. Unfortunately, no such statements are to be found in the Throne Speech.
In a speech delivered by the Minister of Communications (Miss MacDonald) to the Financial Post Conference on Broadcasting on September 29, 1986, she outlined a process which would lead toward the eventual implementation of the Caplan-Sauvageau Report. The Minister stated in her address: "I will be doing everything in my power to ensure that the initiatives emerging from this process will be carried out before the end of this Government's first term of office". One would have expected that the Minister's commitment to implement
some of the Caplan-Sauvageau Report would have found expression in the Throne Speech. Unfortunately, that is not so. It was totally ignored.
The second paragraph on the second to last page of that speech states as follows:
To begin debate on this fundamental challenge, my government will define its objectives and ways to achieve them.
I have two comments about this statement. First, the Government has held power for more than two years. It is about time the Government defined its objectives. Second, I do not understand why the Throne Speech uses the phrase "To begin debate". Surely we have already had considerable debate. Since taking power in 1984 the Government has commissioned nine separate reports to advise it on what it should do in matters of broadcasting and culture. This is most unexpected from a Government which professed, when elected, to have a direct plan of action which it was eager to implement.
I understand that I have run out of time. I would like to conclude by saying that there have been enough studies done by the Government. It is really time for action.
